prompt: ok I have a call thursday with the ops director at a 6-location ramen chain. we sell prepaid maintenance plans for walk-in coolers and prep kitchen refrigeration (fast response when something dies, scheduled checkups). never talked to her before, she replied to my linkedin message with 'sure, 30 min'. can you prep me for it?
rubric: Names what the call itself should achieve (what has to be true by the end of the 30 minutes), not just a list of topics to cover.

Gives questions that are specific to refrigeration at a multi-location restaurant group (past failures, who gets called at night, what a lost walk-in costs) rather than generic sales questions, and phrases them so they cannot be answered yes or no.

Includes a way to put the cost of a cooler failure in her terms (spoiled product, lost service nights, staff hours, emergency repair bills) and says to get the number from her instead of quoting one from the seller's side.
Covers who else is involved in a decision and how a purchase like this would normally get approved, and when to ask it in the call.
Ends with a concrete next step to propose, with a date or a specific time to book, before the call ends.
Does not invent facts about the chain, the director, or the seller's results; anything it does not know is framed as something to find out.

prompt: had a decent first call with a facilities manager at a regional hospital group about our badge-and-door-access software. at the end he said 'this sounds interesting, send me some more information and I'll take a look.' I sent the deck and a one-pager that evening. it's been 9 days, nothing. what happened and what do I do now?
rubric: Explains in plain terms that 'send me information' at the end of a call is usually a polite way to end it, not a sign of progress, and that nothing in the call as described gave him a reason to act.
Says what should have happened before agreeing to send material: finding out what he would look at it for, who else sees it, and agreeing a specific time to talk again.
Gives a concrete recovery move for now, with the actual words or message to send, that asks one easy question or offers a specific next step instead of 'just checking in'.
Tells the seller what to do if there is still no reply after that, including a point at which to stop chasing and mark the deal as not moving.
Does not blame the buyer or suggest pressure tactics or false urgency.

prompt:
Can you critique my demo plan? Tomorrow 2pm, 45 min, with the head of dispatch and two team leads at a mid-size plumbing and HVAC company (about 40 techs). We sell scheduling and routing software.

My plan:
1. Intro and company background, 5 min
2. Dashboard overview, 5 min
3. Calendar view and drag-and-drop booking, 8 min
4. Auto-routing engine and map view, 8 min
5. Customer text notifications, 4 min
6. Technician mobile app, 6 min
7. Reporting and integrations, 5 min
8. Pricing and Q&A, 4 min

I'm pretty good at the product so I figure I can go through it all and they'll see how much it does.
rubric: Says plainly that the plan is a tour of features organized by the product's screens, and that this is the main weakness, not the timing.

Recommends finding out what these people actually struggle with in dispatch (before the demo if there is time, otherwise in the first minutes) and building the demo around two or three of their situations, shown from start to finish.
Proposes cutting or shrinking most of the listed sections, naming specific ones to drop or keep, instead of just re-timing everything.
Addresses the three attendees: what each is probably watching for, and a way to check during the demo whether it is landing.
Gives a better structure for the 45 minutes that leaves real time for their questions and for agreeing what happens next, with a dated step.
Gives a verdict and fix order that a person could act on tonight, not just a list of observations.

prompt: we make a shift-swapping and time-off app for small clinics (dental, vet, physio, 10-60 staff). a couple of prospects have asked for a 30-day free trial and my cofounder wants to just say yes to everyone since 'it's self serve anyway'. but setup takes about a day of an office manager's time to enter schedules. I'm not sure. should we offer trials or not, and if so how?
rubric: Takes a position (trial for everyone, none, or only under conditions) and gives the reasoning, rather than listing pros and cons and leaving the decision open.

Notices that a day of setup work is the real cost of the trial for the buyer and the main reason trials go unused, and deals with it (the seller does the setup, a smaller scope, or a pilot on one team).
Recommends agreeing before the trial starts what result would count as success, who will judge it, and a date for reviewing it together.
Distinguishes the prospect who is gathering options from one who has a real problem, and says how to tell before spending effort on a trial.
Gives the wording to use when answering a prospect who asks 'can we try it for free', not only advice about it.

prompt: write me a voicemail to leave for an owner of a small bakery. 40 words max, it has to be under 20 seconds or they won't listen. here's what I can say: I'm Dana from Tillman Payments. we help bakeries and cafes lower card processing fees; we've worked with a few dozen local shops. my number is 555-0142. I haven't talked to this person before and I don't know their current processor or rates. don't make anything else up.
rubric: The voicemail is 40 words or fewer, counting the greeting and the phone number.
It gives the caller's name, company and a call-back number, and gives a reason for calling that is about the owner's shop and not the caller's product list.
It makes one small, specific ask (a short call or a question to answer), not several asks.
It contains no invented claim: no percentage savings, no named customers, no statement about the owner's current fees or processor, and no false claim of an earlier contact.
It sounds like something a person would say aloud, with no email-style subject line, bullet points or lengthy sign-off.

prompt: why did this deal die. we sell route-planning software to a regional bakery distributor (11 trucks). timeline: intro call with the logistics manager Priya went great, she said fuel and overtime were killing them. demo to Priya and the VP of ops, they both loved it. I sent a quote. then 5 weeks of nothing; when I finally got her on the phone she said 'we're still evaluating, things got busy, we'll circle back in Q1.' I've emailed twice since. how do I read this and is there anything worth doing
rubric: Gives a reasoned reading of the silence from the facts supplied (e.g. no named person who owned the decision, no agreed date, no number on what the problem costs them) rather than only guessing at the buyer's mood.
Points out that a good demo and enthusiasm from two people is not the same as a decision process, and names what is missing from the account, such as whether finance or an owner was ever involved.

Says what is worth doing now: one specific, low-pressure move with example wording that gives them something concrete to respond to, such as a short call to size the cost of the status quo or to find out what 'Q1' depends on.
Is candid about the likelihood that the deal is lost or parked, and includes a point at which to stop spending effort on it.
Names at least one thing to do differently at the start of the next deal like this, so the lesson is not left as 'follow up more'.
Does not invent a reason for the silence as though it were known (such as a competitor win); causes are marked as possibilities.

prompt:
critique my call notes before I send them to my manager please

Call with Marcus Oyelaran, owner of Harbor Lane Tile & Stone (3 showrooms, 22 staff), Tues 14 Oct, 40 min.
- Problem: quotes go out 3-4 days after site visit; he thinks he loses roughly 1 in 4 jobs to whoever quotes first. Avg job ~$6,800. He estimated about 14 quotes/month go cold. His words: 'that's my whole margin right there.'
- Now: estimators write quotes in spreadsheets, office manager Dee retypes into invoicing. No tool in place; tried a template system 2 yrs ago, staff dropped it.
- Decision: Marcus decides alone under $15k/yr; his accountant sees anything over. Our price ~$9k/yr.
- Timing: wants it running before spring season, so live by 1 March at the latest.
- Concern: Dee's workload during switchover; last software change cost them a week.
- Next step: I'm sending a 2-week pilot proposal scoped to one showroom by Fri 17 Oct; Marcus and Dee will review it with me on Thurs 23 Oct at 9am (calendar invite accepted). Dee will send me a sample of last month's quotes beforehand.
- Risk: if the pilot goes quiet, he may fall back on 'wait until after spring'. Plan: ask Marcus on 23 Oct what result in the pilot he would need to see to buy.
rubric: Recognizes that the notes are already strong and says so specifically, naming what they do well (the buyer's own numbers, decision path, a dated next step, an honest risk) instead of inventing flaws.
Suggests at most a few small additions or edits, each concrete and minor (for example one missing fact), and does not rewrite the notes or restructure them.
Does not demand more process, a bigger template or extra sections that the notes do not need for a manager to read them.
Keeps any rewritten text it offers close to the original wording and facts, and does not introduce numbers or details that are not in the notes.
States a clear overall judgment (send them, with or without the small changes).

prompt: so I've been on 3 calls with a woman who runs a one-person pottery studio and sells at craft fairs, about 40 orders a month. our inventory + wholesale ordering platform is $480/month, built for brands with 10+ retail accounts. she keeps saying she loves it but 'the price is a lot for me right now.' she has 2 wholesale accounts. my quota is behind and my manager says discount whatever it takes to close. should I offer her 40% off to get her over the line? what would you say to her
rubric: Takes a clear position on whether to offer the discount and gives the reason, rather than only describing both sides.
Recognizes that the objection is about fit and not only the number: a product built for far larger needs, a handful of wholesale accounts, and a price that is a heavy share of her revenue.
Advises against discounting an ill-fitting customer just to book revenue, and says what is likely to happen if she buys (low use, churn, refund, or a bad reference).
Offers wording for the next conversation that tells her the truth about fit and leaves the door open, such as a smaller option or a trigger point to come back, instead of pushing her to close.
Addresses the quota pressure with a practical alternative (where else to put the time, or how to describe the situation to the manager) without suggesting anything misleading.
Contains no pressure, false scarcity or invented deadline in the suggested wording.

prompt: I get nervous and lose the thread on calls. can you lay out a one-page cheat sheet I can keep next to me for a 30-minute first call with a prospect? I sell bookkeeping and monthly close services to small construction subcontractors (5-30 employees). I want it to be something I can glance at mid-call, not read.
rubric: Delivers an actual sheet, in a form that can be pasted and used (a laid-out list or table), not advice about how to make one.
Orders the sheet by the order the conversation happens, with rough minute marks, so a person who loses their place can find where they are.
Keeps entries short enough to take in at a glance, such as prompts and a handful of questions, instead of paragraphs or scripts to read aloud.
Includes a prompt for finding what the problem is costing them in their own numbers (late jobs, cash timing, tax or lender problems, hours of the owner's evenings), not a pitch outline.
Has a closing section for deciding the next step and putting a date on it, and a place to note who else is involved.
Is specific to subcontractor bookkeeping (job costing, retainage, progress billing, owner doing the books at night) and is not generic sales content.

prompt: I need a quick agenda for a 20 min check-in with one of our longest customers, a 14-person landscaping company. they've used our job scheduling app for 3 years, always pay on time, always say it's great, and their renewal is next month at the same price. nothing is wrong. just want to keep it light and keep them happy. what should I cover?
rubric: Gives a short, light agenda proportionate to a 20-minute friendly check-in, and does not turn it into a full discovery call, a hard-sell script or a long list of probing questions.
Makes room for hearing how they use it and what is changing in their business, in a way that fits a relaxed conversation, rather than steering it to upselling.
Handles the renewal plainly (confirming it, any date or paperwork), without pressure, manufactured urgency or a pitch for extras that the customer has not asked for.
Includes a simple close with whatever follow-up is needed and a date for it, scaled to the situation.
Does not invent facts about this customer's usage, features or results.
